quote: welche [-V-] Veränderung oder Uebergänge von einem Element zu anderen man in Betracht ziehen soll, um z. B. das Analogon für Universalität zu bekommen, ist eine wichtige Frage.
english: Which changes or transitions from one element to others one should consider in order to obtain, e.g., the analogue of universality is an important question.
topic: Hilbert discusses, by analogy with power series expansion and Riemann surfaces, when the linear variation of one solution curve depends uniquely and invertibly on that of another, identifying 'branch elements' as those satisfying the Lagrange differential equation (vanishing of the first variation), and proposes studying curves without inflection points.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert is drawing an analogy with Weierstrass analytic continuation. In that setting, power-series elements are continued into one another until they form a complete analytic function or Riemann surface, the 'universality' of the analytic object. He asks the matching question for extremals of a variational problem. If the 'elements' are solution curves of the Euler–Lagrange equation and they are related through their linear variations (Jacobi fields, the linearisation of the Euler–Lagrange equation), which admissible transitions or deformations between elements should be allowed so that their closure gives a canonical, maximal 'complete' object, an analogue of the complete analytic function? In that picture, the degenerate 'branch elements' would play the role of branch points; in modern terms they are roughly conjugate points or caustics. This is a heuristic, programmatic question rather than a precisely posed problem.
triage.answered_by: No specific answer can be attributed. The broad themes were later developed elsewhere: Jacobi fields and conjugate points in the linearised Euler–Lagrange equation, field-of-extremals theory, Morse theory, and the symplectic/Lagrangian-singularity treatment of conjugate points and caustics. None of these sources is a documented resolution of this particular note.

evidence.claim: In the classical calculus of variations the Jacobi equation is the linearisation of the Euler–Lagrange equation, and conjugate points are defined through it. This is the modern form of the 'linear variation of one solution curve relative to another'.
Generic properties of conjugate points are still studied today in optimal control and the calculus of variations.

Hilbert's 23rd problem is not a specific problem but a general encouragement to develop the calculus of variations. The diary question fits that general spirit but is not one of the published problems.

triage.why: The note does not define 'element', 'transition' or 'universality' precisely enough to match it to any one later theorem or open problem. It is a methodological question about which notion of continuation or deformation would give a variational analogue of Weierstrass's complete analytic function. The search found nothing tying it to Hilbert's published problems. It matches the 23rd problem only in its general aim, as encouragement for the calculus of variations. The related themes (Jacobi fields, conjugate points and caustics, global theory of extremals) were developed extensively later and are still researched. The search did not find a direct source on Lagrangian singularities or Morse theory, so their mention is background only. Whether this exact 'universality' question was ever posed and answered cannot be established from the sources found.
